name: flow-card
description:
One step of a flow that happens away from the main product. THREE screens across TWO services are this shape, which is what made it a unit rather than a component: avenID's device authorisation, my.aven.ceo's name check, and my.aven.ceo's passkey sign-in. Each one is a mark or a status glyph, an eyebrow, a heading, a description, sometimes a code to read aloud, an action, and a line saying who you are talking to.

It is a unit because these are the screens where a user is asked to TRUST something, and every element on them is doing that job. On avenID the status glyph was three hand-drawn inline SVGs in an `{#if}` chain — three chances to drift and no way for another surface to reuse them. On checkout the same screen leads with the brand mark instead, which is why `crest` is a slot: what goes at the top of a trust screen is a decision the surface makes, not one this unit should force.

base.$description:
THE CARD IS THE PAGE. These screens have one thing on them and nothing else, so the card is not a tile in a column of tiles — it floats, and it is sized and lifted accordingly: 32rem wide, a 2rem radius, a wide soft ambient shadow, and a translucent ground with a glass blur so the page's own gradient reads through it.

All of that is recovered, not invented. avenID's cards had it, spelled by hand in that service's app.css; the first pass onto this actor flattened them into a plain 26rem panel with a hairline shadow and a 15px heading. The design was the better one, so it moved in here where all four surfaces get it.

CONTAINER, and the clamps read `cqi` — the card's own width — rather than `vw`. The heading spans `fs-display` to `fs-display-lg` because on a screen with one sentence on it, that sentence is display type.

GAP IS ZERO ON PURPOSE. Each part states the space above it — crest 1.5rem, eyebrow 0.7rem, description 1rem, code 1.75rem, trust 1.6rem — which is how the original set its rhythm. A grid gap on top of those margins adds a step between every pair and the card loses the uneven spacing that made it read as composed rather than stacked.

eyebrow.$description:
Small, heavy and widely tracked.

THE SIZE IS THE ORIGINAL'S, and it is off the type scale. avenID set these by hand — 0.7rem, 0.95rem, 0.65rem, 0.72rem — and the nearest tokens are a step away in each case. Matched to the original rather than rounded to the scale, because these four screens are the ones people judge the product by and the original was better. If the scale should absorb them, that is a change to the scale, not to this card.

heading.$description:
Display type, and the heaviest thing on the screen. One sentence IS the screen here.

`9.1cqi`, not the original's `5vw`: `vw` measured an 800px window, `cqi` measures the card's CONTENT box (414px inside a 512px card), so the multiplier has to be nearly double to land on the same 37.6px. The `0.67em` margin is the browser's own h1 default on BOTH sides, which the original inherited: it sets the space under the crest AND the space above the description. Setting it on the top alone closed the gap under the heading by 26px and the whole card came up short.

description.$description:
The only prose on the screen, at generous leading.

THE SIZE IS THE ORIGINAL'S, and it is off the type scale. avenID set these by hand — 0.7rem, 0.95rem, 0.65rem, 0.72rem — and the nearest tokens are a step away in each case. Matched to the original rather than rounded to the scale, because these four screens are the ones people judge the product by and the original was better. If the scale should absorb them, that is a change to the scale, not to this card.

code.$description: A full-width well holding a label and the value it names. The label sits INSIDE, which is the original's shape: the well is one block that says 'here is the code', not a bare pill with a caption floating above it.

code-label.$description:
What the value below it is.

THE SIZE IS THE ORIGINAL'S, and it is off the type scale. avenID set these by hand — 0.7rem, 0.95rem, 0.65rem, 0.72rem — and the nearest tokens are a step away in each case. Matched to the original rather than rounded to the scale, because these four screens are the ones people judge the product by and the original was better. If the scale should absorb them, that is a change to the scale, not to this card.

code-value.$description: The code itself: mono, widely tracked, in the brand dark. Tracking matters more here than anywhere else in the system — this string gets read aloud down a phone line.

actions.$description:
A full-width row, and a SINGLE action fills it.

That last part is the original's, and it is the difference between a card that closes with a decision and one that closes with a link: avenID's `.device-flow > button` was `width: 100%; min-height: 3.25rem`. Two actions stay auto-width and centred, which is what the checkout's Zurück/Weiter pair was — so `:only-child` carries the distinction rather than a variant the call site has to remember.

trust.$description:
Who you are talking to. Quiet, and set well away from the action.

THE SIZE IS THE ORIGINAL'S, and it is off the type scale. avenID set these by hand — 0.7rem, 0.95rem, 0.65rem, 0.72rem — and the nearest tokens are a step away in each case. Matched to the original rather than rounded to the scale, because these four screens are the ones people judge the product by and the original was better. If the scale should absorb them, that is a change to the scale, not to this card.

crest.$description: A SOLID TILE, not an outlined circle. 4rem square at a 1rem radius, filled with the brand dark and carrying its own lift, so the glyph reads light on dark and the tile sits above the card the way the card sits above the page. The outlined-circle version this replaces was the same shape as every avatar in the system, which is exactly what a status crest must not be.

status.$description: The answer, in one word, at the size the eye lands on first — `taken`, `free`, `expired`. On checkout this was a bare `.status` with `.taken` and `.free` beside it, which is colour carrying the meaning; the WORD carries it here and the colour agrees with it.

How the crest reads. SOLID FILLS, like the default — the original set `.device-flow__icon.success { background: paradise-water }` and `.error { background: terracotta }`, both keeping the light glyph. The first pass made these light surface tints with dark ink, which inverts the tile: a status crest that goes PALER when something fails is the wrong direction, and it stopped matching the marine default sitting beside it in the same flow.

crest.$description: What the crest holds. `brand` drops the tinted disc entirely, because a logo inside a coloured circle is a logo with a badge around it.

answer.$description: The colour agreeing with the word, never replacing it.

step.$description: WHERE in the flow this card is — which is not the same as `status`, which is how it is GOING. Each step tints the eyebrow and the crest with the tone that belongs to it, so the four screens of one sequence are visibly one sequence rather than four cards that happen to look alike. Three of these once declared nothing at all and were documentation wearing a variant's name: a switch that changes nothing is worse than no switch, because it teaches you the control is broken.

identify.$description: Who are you — the name check, the sign-in.

authorise.$description: Do you allow this — the device grant, the consent.

pay.$description: Confirm the money. Marine, because this is the one step that takes something.

a11y.note: `aria-live="polite"` on the card, because the heading and description CHANGE as the flow advances and a screen-reader user is otherwise left on the previous step with no way to know. The alert is `role="alert"`, which interrupts — correct for a failure the user must act on. The status glyph is decorative: colour is never the only signal, so the heading always says in words what the glyph says in shape. The code is `user-select: all` so it can be copied in one gesture rather than dragged. The visual order and the DOM order are the same, so a keyboard tabs to the way out before the commit — which is the safer default when someone is moving fast.
